title: Borrowed Credibility
lines: Borrowed Credibility examines how scientific reputation can substitute for evidence without anyone intending deception.
The book begins from a necessary fact: nobody can independently verify everything they use.
Institutions therefore ration attention through names, affiliations, journals, and previous success.
The danger appears when those shortcuts acquire more authority than their evidence deserves.
Its constructive argument joins scientific incentives with ways to make verification cheaper and more specific.
Readers gain a framework for reforming trust without dismissing expertise or imagining universal corruption.

title: One paper, two pedigrees
lines: The opening follows a composite paper presented with different signals of scientific pedigree.
It is a thought experiment, not a report of one secretly manipulated submission.
The changing reception directs attention toward expectations formed before the evidence is examined.
The book uses this device to ask how credibility travels between people and claims.
Reputation can reasonably guide attention while still distorting the judgment that follows.
That tension anchors the argument instead of reducing it to heroes and villains.

title: When a proxy becomes proof
lines: Scientific cooperation requires shortcuts because independent verification is costly and unevenly distributed.
A respected name or journal can help someone decide where to look first.
The problem begins when that initial guidance becomes a substitute for claim specific evidence.
The book follows this shift from an attention signal toward an apparent verdict.
It asks which part of confidence comes from the work and which from its surroundings.
That question gives readers a practical distinction without demanding that they abandon expertise.

title: Credibility compounds
lines: Credibility can also accumulate through access to resources, collaborators, and further opportunities.
Real achievement may start the process without explaining every advantage that follows.
The book examines how feedback can strengthen both productive expertise and institutional closure.
It keeps merit and cumulative advantage in the same picture.
That balance matters because a simple story of corruption would miss ordinary incentives.
Readers are invited to inspect a system whose participants can behave reasonably within flawed arrangements.

title: Who pays for correction
lines: The middle chapters move from reputation toward the work required to challenge a claim.
Review, replication, and correction consume expertise that institutions may reward only weakly.
Competition can also complicate the relationship between expert assessment and professional interest.
A metric designed to summarize quality can become a target that reorganizes behavior.
The book connects these incentives rather than treating each failure as an isolated scandal.
Its reform question is who will do verification when doing it carries real costs.

title: Trust at claim scale
lines: The constructive chapters propose moving more assessment toward specific claims and their dependencies.
A person's reputation can remain useful without deciding every claim in advance.
Evidence, uncertainty, and correction history would become easier to inspect and update separately.
The book also considers paying for correction and supporting a portfolio of approaches.
These are institutional proposals whose costs and unwanted effects still need evaluation.
Their purpose is to make disagreement actionable without requiring a verdict on an entire career.

title: AI as an assistant
lines: Artificial intelligence enters the argument as a possible way to reduce some assessment costs.
It might assist comparison, evidence tracing, consistency checks, or continuing review.
The book does not treat an automated score as a sovereign scientific verdict.
The same machinery can reproduce status bias or create another opaque authority.
Its role therefore depends on visible procedures and meaningful opportunities for human challenge.
This restraint matters to the book's broader argument about distributing trust without disguising power.

title: Institutions that can revise
lines: Later proposals explore pedigree sensitivity, portable evidence, and confidence that changes with new information.
A counterfactual audit can ask whether altered identity signals change an assessment.
Such sensitivity alone does not prove discrimination in every individual decision.
The book combines diagnostic tools with procedures for challenge, revision, and justified surprise.
It also asks whether new guardians of evidence could become gatekeepers themselves.
Reading these limits is essential to evaluating the reforms rather than merely admiring their intentions.

title: Read beyond the scandal
lines: Start with the composite paper and keep its evidential content separate from its pedigree.
Follow the incentive chapters before turning to the proposed institutions of correction.
The conclusion asks for a better use of trust, not its disappearance.
Borrowed Credibility gives readers a vocabulary for locating specific failures in scientific confidence.
It also provides proposals that deserve pilots, criticism, and revision rather than automatic adoption.
Read it to ask how expertise can remain useful while evidence stays capable of changing minds.
